title: Who was the Ethiopian woman Moses had married, and what was the complaint about her?
summary: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses “because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married”. The woman is not named, the passage does not say when Moses married her, and it does not say what the objection was. The next verse turns to a different matter and she is not mentioned again in the chapter.
text: KJV Numbers 12:1: “And Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married: for he had married an Ethiopian woman.” KJV 12:2: “Hath the Lord indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us?” KJV Exodus 2:16: “Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters” KJV Exodus 2:21: “And Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter.” KJV Exodus 18:2: “took Zipporah, Moses' wife, after he had sent her back” KJV Habakkuk 3:7: “I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction: and the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble.” Hebrew (WLC) Numbers 12:1: עַל־אֹדֹ֛ות הָאִשָּׁ֥ה הַכֻּשִׁ֖ית אֲשֶׁ֣ר לָקָ֑ח כִּֽי־אִשָּׁ֥ה כֻשִׁ֖ית לָקָֽח [on account of the Cushite woman whom he had taken, for he had taken a Cushite woman]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Numbers 12:1: ἕνεκεν τῆς γυναικὸς τῆς Αἰθιοπίσσης ἣν ἔλαβε Μωυσῆς [on account of the Ethiopian woman whom Moses took]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/4/12/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/NUM12.htm.
reasoning: The marriage is given as the occasion of the whole episode, which ends with Miriam leprous and shut out of the camp. Yet the reader is not told who the woman is. The only wife of Moses named in the passages checked is Zipporah, daughter of the priest of Midian. Whether the woman of Numbers 12:1 is Zipporah under another description or a second wife changes what Miriam and Aaron are objecting to, and the passage gives the objection no words: what they are reported as saying is about prophecy.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that she is Zipporah, described by a name that Habakkuk 3:7 sets beside Midian (“Cushan”); that she is a second wife from the land the KJV calls Ethiopia, married after or beside Zipporah; that the complaint was about her people, or about the marriage itself, or was a pretext for the challenge of verse 2. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV finds “Zipporah” in Exodus 2:21, 4:25 and 18:2 only, and “Ethiopian woman” in Numbers 12:1 only; the verses of Numbers 12 quoted here and the rest of that chapter’s sixteen verses were searched for any further mention of her and none was found. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked passages do not explicitly settle who she was or what the objection was. The KJV’s “Ethiopian” stands for the Hebrew word Cushite and agrees with the Greek; no H or G is proposed. A published record on this chapter concerns the different outcomes for Miriam and Aaron, not the woman. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

title: What was “the book of the wars of the Lord”, and where does its quotation end?
summary: Numbers cites a written source by name, “the book of the wars of the Lord”, to support a statement about the border at Arnon. No book of that name is among the books of the KJV, the passage does not say who wrote it or when, and the words quoted from it break off without a finished sentence.
text: KJV Numbers 21:13: “for Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites” KJV 21:14: “Wherefore it is said in the book of the wars of the Lord, What he did in the Red sea, and in the brooks of Arnon,” KJV 21:15: “And at the stream of the brooks that goeth down to the dwelling of Ar, and lieth upon the border of Moab.” KJV Joshua 10:13: “Is not this written in the book of Jasher?” Hebrew (WLC) Numbers 21:14: עַל־כֵּן֙ יֵֽאָמַ֔ר בְּסֵ֖פֶר מִלְחֲמֹ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה [therefore it is said in the book of the wars of the LORD]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Numbers 21:14: Διὰ τοῦτο λέγεται ἐν βιβλίῳ, πόλεμος τοῦ Κυρίου [Therefore it is said in a book: a war of the Lord]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/4/21/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/NUM21.htm.
reasoning: The narrative appeals to another writing as its support (“Wherefore it is said in …”), so what that writing was bears on how the book of Numbers describes its own sources. The passage gives a title and a fragment and nothing else: not the author, not the date, not what else the book held. The fragment in the KJV has no main verb of its own after “What he did”, and the passage does not mark where the quotation stops and the narrative resumes.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that it was a collection of war songs or records now lost; that the title is not a title, and the words “war of the Lord” belong to the quotation, as Brenton’s Greek prints them; that the quotation runs through verse 15, or further. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV for “book of the wars” finds this verse only; Joshua 10:13 is quoted as another place where a narrative cites a named book, not as an answer. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what the book was. The difference between the KJV and the Greek wording of the quotation is a separate record; this record is about the unnamed source only. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. title: Thirty-two persons were the tribute given to Eleazar the priest: what was done with them?
summary: From the Midianite captives, one person in five hundred of the soldiers’ half is levied as tribute and given to Eleazar the priest as a heave offering: thirty-two persons. The passage counts them in the same list and the same words as the sheep, beeves and asses, and does not say what the priest did with them.
text: KJV Numbers 31:28: “one soul of five hundred, both of the persons, and of the beeves, and of the asses, and of the sheep” KJV 31:29: “Take it of their half, and give it unto Eleazar the priest, for an heave offering” KJV 31:30: “thou shalt take one portion of fifty, of the persons, of the beeves, of the asses, and of the flocks, of all manner of beasts, and give them unto the Levites, which keep the charge of the tabernacle” KJV 31:35: “And thirty and two thousand persons in all, of women that had not known man by lying with him.” KJV 31:40: “And the persons were sixteen thousand; of which the” … “tribute was thirty and two persons.” KJV 31:41: “And Moses gave the tribute, which was the” … “heave offering, unto Eleazar the priest” KJV 31:47: “Moses took one portion of fifty, both of man and of beast, and gave them unto the Levites” Hebrew (WLC) 31:40: וּמִכְסָם֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה שְׁנַ֥יִם וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֖ים נָֽפֶשׁ [and their levy for the LORD: thirty-two souls]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 31:40: καὶ τὸ τέλος αὐτῶν Κυρίῳ, δύο καὶ τριάκοντα ψυχαί [and their tax for the Lord, thirty-two souls]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/4/31/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/NUM31.htm.
reasoning: The passage is exact about the count and silent about the outcome. Persons are levied by the same rule as the animals, called by the same two words (“tribute”, “heave offering”), and handed to the priest. For the larger share given to the Levites the passage adds that the Levites “keep the charge of the tabernacle”; for the thirty-two given to Eleazar it adds nothing. What it means for a person to be the tribute handed to the priest is left unstated.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that the thirty-two became servants of the priest or of the sanctuary; that they were held as the priest’s property like the rest of his portion; or that “heave offering” here means the same for persons as for animals. This record does not assert any of them. Check made: Numbers 31:26–30, 31:35–37, 31:40–41 and 31:47 were read; the packaged KJV has the word “tribute” in Numbers only in 31:28 and 31:37–41. That is a word search and part of one chapter, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not say what was done with the persons. A published record on this chapter notes in general that the later treatment of the captives is not specified; this record places the question on the two verses about the priest’s thirty-two. The Hebrew and the Greek quoted agree with the KJV; no H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text.
